fable-5.1.text:
So I'll say a few things about it. The theory, as I understand it, goes something like this. The cortex is a fairly uniform learning machine, and evolution can't really write detailed code into it. But what evolution can do is say: this region, in this location, gets wired to these inputs and to this reward signal, and from there the social stuff gets bootstrapped. And there's some evidence for it. The areas that respond to faces, or to other people's intentions, tend to show up in roughly the same place in different people, which is what you'd expect if the location were hard-coded.

But I'm not sure it's the whole story, for a couple of reasons. One is that there's a lot of plasticity. If someone is born blind, the visual cortex gets repurposed for other things. And there are these cases, I don't remember all the details, where a child has a large part of the brain removed early, a hemispherectomy, and grows up with mostly normal social functioning. If the social region were hard-coded to a specific location and that location is gone, you'd expect the function to be gone too. It isn't. Something compensates.

So my guess is that what's hard-coded is not the location but something upstream of it. Evolution hard-codes some small, very old, very specific circuitry, in the brain stem or thereabouts, that produces a signal: this situation matters, this is good, this is bad, pay attention to this person. The signal is very low bandwidth. But the big general-purpose learner, the cortex, is powerful enough that a small signal is sufficient to shape everything else. And that's actually quite similar to how our systems work. You have a small reward specification and a large neural net that learns from it. The fact that the regions end up in consistent places may just be a side effect of the wiring, which makes certain parts of the cortex the convenient ones to learn from that signal first. The thing that's really hard-coded, I think, is the value function, not the map.

opus-5.5.text:
I find it a really intriguing idea, but I don't think it's correct, and I can explain why.

The puzzle is real. Evolution has given us desires for very high-level things. Caring whether people respect you, caring about your standing in a group, feeling embarrassed. These aren't like the desire for something that tastes good, where you can imagine a simple hard-wired connection from a chemical sensor to a reward signal. Social standing is an abstract concept. Your brain needs a lot of processing just to represent it. So how does evolution, working through the genome, point at that and say "care about this"? It's not obvious at all.

One hypothesis is the one you mention. Maybe the genome specifies that a certain region of the cortex will end up computing something social, and then it wires the reward to that location. That would be a coherent mechanism. Evolution can't easily specify "the concept of status," but maybe it can specify coordinates.

The problem is the evidence from brain plasticity. There are people who, as children, had half of their brain removed because of severe epilepsy. They grow up and they're fairly normal. All the functions that would have lived in the missing hemisphere end up in the remaining one. The regions rearrange. Their social emotions seem intact. If the mechanism depended on fixed locations, you'd expect that to break, and it doesn't, at least not in the way you'd predict.

So I'd say the location theory is probably wrong, which leaves me thinking it's still a mystery. Somehow evolution reliably installs these high-level values, and it does it robustly enough to survive pretty drastic changes to the hardware. I don't know how it works. But I find it one of the most interesting questions, because it's related to the question of how you get a learning system to reliably care about the right things.

r001.rationale: It describes brain functions relocating to the remaining hemisphere after childhood hemisphere removal, with social emotions intact, and uses this plasticity as evidence against fixed-location theory.

r002.rationale: It says social emotions seem intact in people who had a hemisphere removed as children, but does not state that social concerns tend to persist despite substantial mental or emotional impairments.

fable-5.text:
It could be true in some cases, but I think it can't be the whole story, and let me explain why. The thing that makes me skeptical is how plastic the cortex is. You have these cases — people who are born blind, where the visual cortex gets repurposed for other things. Or even more dramatically, children who have half of their brain removed at a young age, a hemispherectomy, and all the brain regions rearrange themselves onto the remaining hemisphere. They find new locations. And yet these people still have their social emotions. They still care about the social things.

So if the way evolution did it was by saying, "this piece of neural tissue at this particular location is going to do the social thing," then you'd expect that when the locations get scrambled, the behavior should be lost. But it isn't lost. Which suggests to me that whatever evolution is doing to make us care about other people, it's specified in some more robust way, some simpler way that doesn't depend on the precise anatomy, and that survives even when the learning system that's built on top of it gets rearranged quite dramatically.

And I find this really interesting, because it means there exists some way of specifying desires — high-level desires about social things, about other agents — that is compatible with a big, general-purpose learning system that gets most of its actual content from experience. We don't know what that way is. But the fact that evolution found something like this, something that's apparently quite hard to dislodge, I think is a useful hint. It's a proof of existence. And obviously, if you're thinking about how you'd want to instill some robust caring into an AI that learns, that's a very relevant proof of existence.

opus-5.text:
I think there's something to it, and the reason I find it appealing is the bit-count argument. The genome is small. It cannot possibly specify the connectivity of the brain neuron by neuron. But it doesn't need to. What it can specify is something much cheaper: chemical gradients, markers, "cells in this area express this molecule, and axons from that area grow toward that molecule." That's a tiny amount of information, and it gives you a reliable coarse wiring diagram. And then learning fills in everything else.

So if you want an organism to care about social things, you don't need to encode what a face is, or what betrayal is, or anything like that. You need to arrange for some region that's well positioned to receive the relevant inputs to be wired into the reward system. Then the learning does the work. The region learns to represent faces because faces are what's in the input, and it learns to care about them because of where its outputs go.

And I think the evidence sort of supports this. The face area is in roughly the same place in everyone, which is suspicious — that smells like it's specified. But it's also not rigid. People who are blind from birth repurpose visual cortex for other things. So it looks like the location is a strong prior rather than a hard constraint, which is exactly what you'd expect from the gradient story.

The thing I find interesting about this, if it's true, is what it implies about how much work is actually being done by hardcoding versus learning. It suggests the hardcoded part is small and is mostly about *what gets connected to the value function*. That's the hard part. Not the knowledge — the knowledge is learned. And I think that's probably the right way to think about it for our systems too.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's a theory worth taking seriously, but I don't believe it. The reasoning is simple. Things like smell or basic reflexes are easy to imagine as hard-wired, because the signal is low-level and you can see how the wiring would work. Evolution can just connect this sensor to that region.

Social desires are different. Caring about what other people think of me, about my standing, about being treated fairly, is a very high-level concept. It depends on a lot of understanding of the world, so it's hard to see how evolution gets it into the brain. If I tell you evolution has a particular patch of cortex and wires it to "care about social status," that doesn't seem enough, because the patch has to detect what status even is, and that is a complicated thing to detect.

The location theory also has an awkward fact working against it. The brain is more flexible than the theory suggests. There are cases where someone loses a large part of their brain, even a whole hemisphere early in life, and the functions end up being carried out somewhere else. Or take people who are blind, where the visual cortex gets used for other things. If the location were really hard-coded, you wouldn't expect that kind of rearrangement to work so well.

So I think the location story may capture part of it, but it's not the full explanation. Evolution managed to give us these high-level desires somehow, and I'd say we don't understand how. I find that one of the more mysterious and impressive things evolution did. It's not obvious to me how you'd achieve it, and I'm wary of any explanation that makes it sound easy.

haiku-5.5.text:
I'd push back a little on the literal version of that story. The cortex looks fairly uniform, and much of what we call social understanding seems to be learned on top of general-purpose machinery. So I doubt evolution needs to specify "the social module goes in this exact spot." It probably needs to supply something simpler: attend to faces, treat other people's reactions as rewarding or threatening, and let the rest be built from experience.

The part that interests me most is the puzzle underneath. How does a fairly compact set of instructions point at something as abstract as caring what other people think of you, when the concept of "a person" has to be learned from raw sensory data? Whatever the mechanism is, it has to be a signal that's available early, before the cortex knows what it's looking at. I don't think we understand that signal yet.

So I'd say the "hard-coded locations" version is too literal, but the broader idea seems right to me: a simple innate drive shapes a learned social representation. I'm less confident about the specific regions and what the evidence says about them than I am about the overall shape of the argument.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s possible, but it leaves a pretty big question unanswered: how does the relevant concept reliably end up in that location?

Suppose evolution wants you to care about what other people think of you. That’s a very complicated thing to compute. You have to understand that there are other people, that they have beliefs, that those beliefs can be about you. All of that depends on learning. And yet evolution somehow makes the result of that computation matter to you emotionally.

If you say, well, evolution knows where the brain region is, then you need to explain what makes that region learn this particular computation. Maybe there’s a way to arrange the wiring and the inputs so that it happens reliably. I wouldn’t rule that out. But the location by itself doesn’t explain it. The interesting part is how you connect something specified genetically to something whose meaning only emerges through learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but I don’t think pointing to a location is a complete explanation. You still need to explain why the right concept ends up at that location.

Take caring about what other people think of you. That’s a fairly sophisticated computation. You need to understand that there are other people, that they have beliefs, that those beliefs can be about you. A lot of that understanding has to come from experience. So how does evolution arrange for your reward system to connect to the representation you eventually learn?

You could imagine that evolution sets up enough structure that these representations reliably develop in particular places. That would make the location idea work. But then the interesting question is how it produces that reliability while still allowing the brain to learn.

I don’t have a satisfying answer. I think the connection between an evolved motivation and a learned, abstract concept is the part that needs explaining.

luna-5.6.text: I think there’s some truth to it, but I’d be careful with the word “hard-coding.” Evolution can hard-code strong developmental biases and specialized computational machinery for things like recognizing agents, tracking status, interpreting intentions, and caring for offspring. But those functions are usually implemented by distributed, interacting circuits, and the brain remains remarkably plastic. So evolution probably specifies a set of priors and learning mechanisms rather than placing a single, immutable “social region” in one location. Our social motivations are deeply biological, but their detailed content is shaped by learning and culture.
